title: QR File Transfer
summary: Move original files across an optical link by displaying a sequence of QR frames on one screen and reconstructing those frames in a receiving browser. The receiver accepts camera frames, images or a recording. The prepared browser candidate is private; the original NAS installation additionally has owner backup functions and native sender packages, which are not included in this candidate.
features: Transfer documents, archives, images and arbitrary binary files; reconstruction verifies the original bytes.
Prepare selected files and display repeated encoded frames; controls support timing and presentation.
Read through a camera or supported image/video input.
Redundant frames allow progress despite missed, reordered or duplicate frames.
Retain partial progress in browser storage for the same transfer identity.
Owner-only resumable file backup into protected NAS storage.
Python and PowerShell alternatives for an already permitted runtime.
workflows: Open the sender page on the sending computer. Use the included harmless hello.txt example before trying a large archive.
Select the intended files and prepare the transfer. Check the filenames and total size; preparation and actual optical transfer are separate stages.
Keep the receiver ready before starting the animation. Set a display size and pace that remain sharp and legible on the receiving camera.
Start the QR sequence. Avoid window overlap, screen dimming and reflection. Esc stops presentation; restarting the display is not the same as changing the file set.
Open receiver.html through an HTTPS origin when using a phone camera. Grant camera access deliberately and point it squarely at the sender display.
Keep the full QR inside the camera frame. Watch progress rather than expecting each visible frame to decode. Missed or duplicate frames are normal.
When reconstruction finishes, save the verified originals. Open a small received file to confirm the expected result before committing to a longer transfer.
For image or recording input, choose the appropriate receiver input instead of live camera capture. The same reconstruction and completion checks still apply.
Return using the same browser and origin that holds the saved progress. Do not clear site storage or use a private browsing session expecting persistence.
Resume the original transfer rather than preparing a different file selection under a similar filename. Stable identity matters.
Check free storage before continuing. Partially received data and reconstructed output can require additional space.
If progress stalls, improve focus, lighting and framing or reduce presentation speed. Do not assume a faster animation increases useful throughput.
Choose whether optical transfer suits the job
Try representative small files and measure actual receive progress on your devices.
Use that measured rate to judge a large job. Multi-gigabyte optical transfers can take days, and mobile browsers may suspend background tabs.
Keep both pages visible and powered during a long transfer. Use the original hosted NAS-backup workflow only when you specifically intend an upload to that NAS.
limits: Protocol tests reconstructed 2,337,225 bytes across three files with dropped, reversed and duplicate frames. Build and timing tests passed. Physical camera throughput, cross-phone compatibility and a 4 GB transfer have not been validated. This project must remain private until separately authorised.
